# Preface

...of diseases deemed incurable (according to the judgment of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the ancient authority on medicine whose theories were often challenged by the new chemical physicians of the Renaissance.</note>), having fundamentally removed their dire and long-standing wounds, he left behind a **Cure** most worthy of eternal memory—to say nothing of the countless proofs of the transmutation of metals. 

We have had, until now, several faithful disciples and followers of Theophrastus <note>Referring to Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss-German physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> who, with great acclaim and success, have cured even more desperate diseases. Innumerable examples of those cured testify to this everywhere—not only in Germany, but also in Italy, France, Belgium, and England. Furthermore, the books written on the expansion and true explanation of this most noble science are outstanding and nearly beyond counting. 

Among others, however, there came to our attention last year a certain Hermetic philosopher <note>A practitioner of "Hermetic" philosophy, which sought to understand the divine laws of nature through alchemy and spiritual study.</note> of Polish nationality <note>This likely refers to Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist known for his influential writings.</note>. He is a man not only of noble lineage and a famous name, but also of the most skillful intellect. Through the instruction and guidance of a certain Arabian master, and with the breath of Divine mercy, he progressed so far as to ascend the venerable **Mountain of Grace** and successfully reach its very highest peaks. Indeed, he was made a partaker of the "Golden Fleece" in the "Garden of the Hesperides" <note>Classical mythological references used here as alchemical allegories for the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> and attained the supreme treasure of the **Blessed Philosopher’s Stone**. This is clearly and undoubtedly certain to us, as can be easily gathered from his small book recently published. This truly **Golden Booklet** [is written] with such clarity—at least as far as the <term>Philosophical Oath</term> <note>original: "Juramentum Philosophicum"; a traditional vow taken by alchemists to keep the core secrets of the "Great Work" hidden from the uninitiated or the greedy.</note> allowed for the disclosure of such secrets...

# Preface

<page-num>387</page-num>

...and it is written with such easy brevity and wonderful skill that, in my judgment, it deserves to be said not only to equal the writings of all other philosophers, but rather to far surpass them. In the meantime, there arrived a *Philosophical Dialogue* by the same Pole <note>Likely Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), whose "Dialogus Mercurii, Alchymistae et Naturae" became a cornerstone of alchemical literature.</note>, witty and fruitful, which was shared with me by a friend in Augsburg <note>Augusta Vindelicorum, a major hub for Renaissance banking and book printing.</note> last year. I decided to attach it to these present booklets concerning the **Philosophers' Stone** <term>Philosophers' Stone: The legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine.</term>, and to publish it, adorned with this preceding praise of the author. 

I wish to faithfully commend this Dialogue to you—as sons of doctrine—not so much to seriously and gently draw your noble minds away from the study of pagan and Aristotelian philosophy practiced until now <note>Figulus and other Paracelsians often rejected the "Heathen" Aristotelian logic taught in universities in favor of chemical and spiritual experience.</note>, but rather to provide a unique spur and incentive for you and others to visit the most holy inner sanctuaries of Hermetic—nay, even Celestial—**TRUTH** and **WISDOM**. Thus, I faithfully advise all scholars, as well as the fellow countrymen of the aforementioned Pole, that they should not fear to follow and linger in these most praiseworthy footsteps; an act for which, as far as I know, no regret will ever enter your minds. 

Farewell, and in Christ, may you happily enjoy this Dialogue, here presented and published in Latin (and in German with me as translator). Farewell again. Written in haste in the noble city of Frankfurt, September 23, in the year 1607.

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER

->S. P. D.<-
<note>Latin: *Salutem Plurimam Dicit*, a formal greeting meaning "Sends fondest greetings."</note>

Stop asking, friend reader, who the author of this little treatise might be. As for why I have published it, <note>original: *conscripserim*—literally "written," but in this context of an editor presenting another's work, it refers to the act of compiling or putting it into print.</note> take this as the reason. It is also not necessary for you to know who I am. Know, however, for an absolute certainty, that the author of this little work perfectly understands, has made, and possesses the **Philosophers' Stone** <term>Philosophers' Stone: A legendary alchemical substance said to be capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</term>. 

Since we are joined by a mutual and sincere goodwill, I asked him—as a sign of my love (as the title itself testifies)—to discuss the **Three Principles**, namely **MERCURY**, **SULFUR**, and **SALT**. I requested that he explain whether the **Philosophers' Stone** should be sought in these common substances or in others, and that he do so using the simplest words and a very modest style. After he had granted my request with this quickly written little treatise, I was firmly convinced that by publishing it or sharing it with others, lovers of **True Philosophy** <note>original: *Verae Philosophiae*. In this era, "philosophy" often referred to natural science and alchemy.</note> would be grateful to me (even if I hope this act is not too displeasing to the author, for he is far removed from all ambition). 

I have no doubt that by reading and carefully considering this work, they will suffer less loss, expense, and damage from impostors, and waste less of their time, reputation, and honor. If I find the honest world—for I hate and keep at a distance the profane mob of **Alchemists** <note>The author distinguishes between "true" alchemical philosophers and "puffers" or fraudulent alchemists seeking only quick wealth.</note>—to be grateful for my benevolent spirit, I will strive to ensure that the remaining two principles and many more things from the same author follow. Meanwhile, enjoy this and farewell, etc.

->A. R. N. P. D.<-

## DIALOGUE BETWEEN NATURE, MERCURY, AND THE ALCHEMIST.

In that time, the Alchemists <note>original: *Chymistæ*</note> gathered together and held a council regarding how they ought to make and prepare the **PHILOSOPHERS’ STONE** <term>Philosophers' Stone: A legendary alchemical substance said to be capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</term>; and so, they decided that each person should state his own opinion by vote. This assembly took place in the open air in a certain meadow on a clear day. Many agreed that **MERCURY** was its **Primary Matter** <term>Primary Matter: Known as *Materia Prima*, this is the original, chaotic substance from which alchemists believed all things were formed.</term>, while others argued for **Sulfur**, and others for other substances. But the majority opinion favored Mercury, especially because of the sayings of the Philosophers, since they hold it to be the true primary matter, and also the primary matter of the **Metals**. For the Philosophers cry out, "Our Mercury," etc. 

And while they were contending among themselves in this way about their various labors—for each of them waited with longing and joy for the conclusion—a massive storm suddenly arose with squalls, clouds, and an unheard-of wind, which scattered that gathering into various provinces, driving everyone away separately without a conclusion. Yet each of them had impressed upon his mind what the end of that dispute ought to be. Therefore, each began his labors as before, one seeking the **Philosophers' Stone** in this thing, another in that; and this continues to this day without ceasing. 

One of them, however, remembering the dispute and that the Stone must necessarily be sought in Mercury, said to himself: "Even if no conclusion was reached, I will nonetheless work in Mercury, and I myself will bring it to a conclusion by creating the **Blessed Stone** <note>original: *Lapide Benedicto*</note>." For he was a man,

who was always accustomed to speak to himself, as Alchemists are wont to do. He began, therefore, to read the books of the Philosophers, and he fell upon the book of Alanus <note>Alanus de Insulis (Alain de Lille), a medieval scholar to whom several alchemical treatises were attributed.</note>, which treats of **Mercury** <note>original: *☿io*</note>; and thus he became an Alchemist-Philosopher without a conclusion <note>That is, he became a "philosopher" in name only, without achieving any results.</note>. Having obtained some Mercury, he began to work; he placed it in a glass vessel and applied fire. The Mercury, as is its custom, evaporated. The wretched Alchemist, being ignorant of its nature, beat his wife, saying: "No one could have come in here but you! You have taken the Mercury out of my glass!" The wife, weeping, defended herself, and said quietly to her husband: "You will make nothing but dung out of these things."

The Alchemist took the Mercury once again and put it back into the vessel; so that his wife would not take it, he guarded it himself. But the Mercury, in its own way, evaporated again. The Alchemist, remembering that the **Primary Matter** <term>Primary Matter: Known as *Materia Prima*, the original substance of all things which alchemists sought to isolate.</term> of the **Philosophers' Stone** must be volatile, rejoiced greatly. Convincing himself entirely that he could no longer be deceived now that he possessed this matter, he began to treat the Mercury boldly. He later learned to sublime it and to calcine <term>Calcine: To reduce a substance to a powder through high heat.</term> it in wondrous ways—now with salts, now with sulfur, now with metals, now with minerals, now with blood, with hair, with **strong waters** <term>Strong waters: Corrosive mineral acids like nitric acid.</term>, now with herbs, urine, and vinegar. But he could find nothing that suited his purpose; he left nothing in the world untouched with which he did not treat the "good" Mercury.

And when he was unable to accomplish anything at all, he came across the saying that [the Stone] "is found in the dunghill." He then began to treat the Mercury with various types of dung, both together and separately. When he had become thoroughly exhausted and full of anxious thoughts, he fell asleep. And in his sleep, a vision appeared to him. An **Old Man** <note>original: *Vir Senex*; in alchemical literature, the "Old Man" often represents a guide or the personification of ancient wisdom.</note> came to him, who greeted him and said: "Friend, why are you so sad?" He responded: "I would very gladly make the Philosophers' Stone."

# Mercury and the Alchemist

Then he [the Old Man] said: "Friend, from what do you wish to make the **Philosophers' Stone**?" <term>Philosophers' Stone: Latin *Lapis Philosophorum*, the legendary substance believed to be capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</term>

ALCHEMIST: "From **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>, Lord."

OLD MAN: "But from what kind of **Mercury**?"

ALCHEMIST: "There is but one **Mercury** <note>original: *☿us*</note>."

OLD MAN: "It is true that there is one **Mercury**, but it varies in different places: one part is purer than another."

ALCHEMIST: "O Lord, I know how to purify it perfectly, with vinegar and saltpeter, and vitriol." <term>Vitriol: A historical term for various sulfate minerals (like copper or iron sulfate), used by alchemists as a powerful acidic agent.</term>

OLD MAN: "I tell you, this purification is not true, nor is this the true **Mercury**. For wise men have another **Mercury** and another way of purifying it." And with that, he vanished.

Waking from his sleep, the Alchemist pondered what that vision meant; he thought about what that **Philosophers' Mercury** should be, but he could conceive of nothing else but his own **common Mercury**. Yet he desired that he might have spoken longer with that Old Man; nevertheless, he now worked diligently, experimenting with the dung of animals and children, and afterwards he even began to work with his own dung <note>It was a common, though misguided, alchemical practice to experiment with "base" organic materials, following the theory that the "Primal Matter" could be found in things most people find repulsive.</note>. 

And every day he went to the place where he saw the vision, so that he might speak to that old man again. Sometimes he would feign sleep, lying with closed eyes waiting for the old man; but when the figure would not come, the Alchemist thought he was afraid, or did not believe that he was sleeping. He swore, saying: "My Lord Old Man, do not be afraid; surely I am sleeping! Look at my eyes, if you do not believe me." 

And that wretched Alchemist, after so much labor and the consumption of all his goods, now fell into a delirium from constantly thinking about that old man. And from that most powerful imagination, a phantom appeared to him in his sleep in the form of **Saturn** <note>original: *♄us* (Saturnus). In alchemy, Saturn is the planetary association for Lead and is often depicted as a slow, wise, or melancholy old man.</note>, an old man, and said to him: 

"Do not despair, friend; your **Mercury** is good, and your matter is good, but if it will not obey you, you must conjure it so that it is not volatile. Even snakes are accustomed to being conjured; why not **Mercury**?"

### Dialogue of Nature

And so the Old Man wished to depart. But the Alchemist pleaded, "Lord, wait!" and in his shouting, the poor wretch was woken. **ALCHEMIST.** "Why then did you refuse to obey me, and why could I not fix you?" <term>Fix: In alchemy, "fixation" is the process of turning a volatile, liquid substance into a solid that can withstand fire without evaporating.</term>

**MERCURY.** "Most certainly, my Lord, I see that your magnificent Lordship is a most excellent Philosopher."

# Mercury and the Alchemist

...he says in a terrible voice: "Well then, now be obedient, otherwise things will not go well for you."

**MERCURY.** "I easily believe it. For it is fitting for such 'Philosophers' to be—those who go insane through excessive prudence and labor."

**ALCHEMIST.** "Come then, tell me: what should I do with you? How shall I make the Philosophers' Stone <term>Philosophers' Stone: Latin *Lapis Philosophicus*. The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</term> out of you?"

**MERCURY.** "O my Lord Philosopher, I do not know. You are the Philosopher, and I am the servant of the Philosophers; whatever they wish to do with me, let them do it. I obey them as much as I am able."

**ALCHEMIST.** "You must tell me how I ought to proceed with you, and if I can make the Philosophers' Stone from you."

**MERCURY.** "If you know how, you will do it; but if you do not know, you will do nothing. You will learn nothing from me if you do not know it beforehand, my Lord..."

...you mix me with dung. **ALCHEMIST.** I do nothing outside of nature, but I sow seed in its own earth, just as the Philosophers have said. **MERCURY.** You sow me in dung, and at the time of the harvest, I vanish, while you are accustomed to reaping nothing but dung. **ALCHEMIST.** Yet the Philosophers wrote thus: that their material ought to be sought in the dungheap. <note>original: *in sterquilinio*. ...the like; I die indeed when I am killed, but I rise again for judgment before a wise Judge. <note>This refers to the alchemical process of "death" (calcination or dissolution) and "resurrection" (sublimation or reconstitution), overseen by the "Judge" (the skilled alchemist or Nature herself).</note> **ALCHEMIST.** Therefore, are you the **Philosophers' Stone**? <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapis Philosophorum*. # Mercury & The Alchemists

...of my heart knows, he sees that **fire** <note>original: *ignem (calorem debitum)*; literally "fire (the proper heat)." Alchemists believed specific, controlled temperatures were required for successful transmutation.</note> is my food. The longer the **SPIRIT** of my heart consumes this Fire, the fatter he will become; his death afterward is the life of all things that dwell in this kingdom where I am. **ALCHEMIST.** Are you Great? **MERCURY.** You have me as an example: from a thousand little drops I shall become one, and from one I can give many thousands of drops. And just as my body is visible before your eyes, if you know how to play with me, you can divide me into as many parts as you wish, and I will become one again. What, then, is the Spirit (**MY HEART**) inwardly? It is that which always brings forth many thousands from the smallest part. **ALCHEMIST.** And how, then, must one work with you so that you become thus? **MERCURY.** I am Fire within; **FIRE** is my food. Indeed, the life of **FIRE** is Air; without Air, fire is extinguished. Fire dominates air. Therefore I do not rest, nor can raw air restrain me. Add air to air, so that both are **ONE**, and they hold weight. Join this with hot fire, and give it to the proper times to guard. **ALCHEMIST.** What will happen afterward? **MERCURY.** The superfluous will be removed; you shall burn the residue with fire, place it in water, and cook it. Afterward, you shall give the cooked result to the sick as **Medicine**. <note>The "Medicine of the Third Order" or the "Universal Panacea" was the medicinal form of the Philosophers' Stone, believed to cure all ailments.</note> **ALCHEMIST.** You tell me nothing that answers my questions! I see that you are only accustomed to mocking me with your parables. Wife! Bring me some **pig dung**; <note>original: *stercus porcinum*. Animal dung was frequently used in alchemy as a source of gentle, consistent heat (through fermentation/decay) for "digestion" or long-term incubation of a substance.</note> I will treat this Mercury in new ways until he tells me how the **Philosophers' Stone** is to be made from him. **MERCURY**, having heard these things, begins to lament over the Alchemist. Why do you torture him, who wishes to do every good for you, if only you were willing to understand? **ALCHEMIST.**

# Dialogue of Nature,

**ALCHEMIST.** What Devil rebukes me, such a great man and **Philosopher**? **NATURE.** O fool; you are a heap of pride, a mere excrement of philosophers. I know the true Philosophers and all the wise ones, whom I love, for they also love me; they do everything according to my pleasure, and where I cannot reach, they assist me. You Alchemists, however—of whose order you are one—act without my knowledge or consent; indeed, you do everything contrary to me. For this reason, the opposite of what you desire happens to you. You think that you treat my children <note>original: *filios meos*; in alchemical theory, "Nature's children" refer to the metals and minerals found in the earth.</note> well, but you accomplish nothing. If you wished to consider the matter correctly, you do not manage them; rather, they manage you. For you can make nothing from them, nor do you know how; indeed, they make fools of you whenever they wish. 

**ALCH.** It is not true! I also am a Philosopher, and I know how to work well. I have served more than one Prince, and I was a Philosopher to them, as my wife well knows. Even now I possess a manuscript book <note>The "hidden manuscript" found in a wall is a common trope in alchemical literature, used to grant the author authority.</note> that was hidden in a wall for several hundred years; now I shall certainly know how to create the **Philosophers' Stone**. Moreover, in these very days, it was revealed to me through a dream. O, I am accustomed to having true dreams—Wife, do you not know this? 

**NATURE.** You will do just as your other colleagues do, who in the beginning know everything—or think they know—but in the end, know nothing. 

**ALCH.** Yet others are accustomed to creating it from you (if you are indeed true nature). 

**NAT.** It is true: but only those who have known me, and they are few. He who truly knows me does not torture my children, nor does he hinder me, but rather acts according to my pleasure; he increases my goods and heals the bodies of my children. 

**ALCH.** Yet I also do this. 

**NAT.** You do all things contrary to me! You proceed against my will with my children; where you ought to **revivify** <note>original: *revivificare*; the process of restoring a metal to its metallic state from an oxide or salt.</note>, you kill; where you ought to **fix**, you **sublimate** <note>original: *sublimas*; to heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then becomes solid again, often used to purify, but Nature here argues it is used incorrectly.</note>; where you ought to **calcine**, you **distill**. This is especially true of this most obedient son of mine, **Mercury**, whom you [harass] with so many **corrosive waters** <note>original: *corrosivis aquis*; strong mineral acids like nitric acid or aqua regia, which Nature views as "torture" compared to gentle, natural heat.</note>, so many—

...torture them with poisonous things? **ALCHEMIST.** Then I shall proceed with him gently, by means of <term>digestion</term> <note>original: *digestionem*; in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of exposing a substance to gentle, consistent heat over a long period, mimicking the biological process of a stomach.</note> alone. **NATURE.** That is well, if you know how; if not, you will harm not him, but yourself and your purse. He is ONE, ONE of the SEVEN <note>original: *UNUS ex SEPTEM*; This refers to the seven metals known to the ancient world, each associated with a celestial body: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Mercury (Mercury), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), and Lead (Saturn).</note>: and he is the FIRST; He is also EVERYTHING; EVERYTHING, I say, he is. He is a Man, yet he acts the part of a Woman: He is a Boy, and carries a man's weapons: He is an Animal, yet he has a bird's <unclear>wings</unclear>: He is a Poison, yet he cures leprosy <note>original: *lepram*; Alchemists often described "base" or impure metals as "leperous." To cure the leprosy of metal was to refine it into pure gold.</note>. He is Life, yet he kills all things; He is a King, yet another possesses his Kingdom; He flees from **Fire**, and yet **Fire** is prepared from him; He is Water, and does not wet; He is Earth, and yet he is <unclear>sown</unclear>: He is Air, and he lives in water. **ALCH.** Now I see that I know nothing, but I do not dare to say so; for I would lose my good reputation, and my neighbor would no longer vouch for me if he knew that I know nothing. I will therefore say that I certainly know, otherwise no one would give me so much as a crust of bread: for many of them hope for many good things from me. **NAT.** And if you prolong this for a long time, what [will you gain] after—
